items.title: How Online Maps Lay Bare the US Military Bases Targeted by Iran
items.summary: Sign up here to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published . Become a member and support our work here . In September, CBS News obtained new images of the aftermath of attacks on US bases in the Middle East from active service members. One told the news channel : “This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public. “We’re standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face,” they added. While reports have detailed how Iran used Russian intelligence , including satellite imagery , to identify US troops, ships and aircraft, Bellingcat found that publicly available mapping platforms also reveal detailed and potentially sensitive information about US military bases in the Middle East. Google Maps and other online mapping services contain dozens of labels identifying facilities including headquarters, accommodation, gyms and fuel points. Publicly available photographs and videos, including material published by the US military, provide further details about how these facilities are used. Experts told Bellingcat that such information could have helped inform Iranian targeting decisions by revealing where personnel gather and how bases operate. However, they cautioned that Iran would also have had access to other sources of intelligence. Reporting from Reuters earlier this year also highlighted how US officials believed commercially available location data was being used to target US troops in war zones. The bases examined by Bellingcat are not secret and have operated for years in a region where US forces maintained a strong sense of security. Joseph Jarnecki, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute , said the US had been able to maintain aerial superiority and was understood to have significant air defence capabilities, but that Iran’s missile and drone campaign has undermined both assumptions. Iranian strikes have damaged at least 20 US military sites across Qatar, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq and Saudi Arabia since the conflict began in February this year. Governments can request that Google blur or remove sensitive information from its services and Google publishes data on government requests for content removal. Bellingcat contacted the US Department of Defense who asked us to reach out to CENTCOM about the details in this story. We also contacted Google. However, we did not receive responses to questions from these respondents before publication. We examined four of the largest and most heavily affected US military installations by Iran’s missile and drone campaign: Camp Buehring and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait, Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan and Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. At each one, we found publicly available Google Maps information providing details about facilities inside the bases and how they are used. A map detailing four US bases that were attacked by Iran during 2026 conflict. Camp Buehring At Camp Buehring in Kuwait, Google Maps identifies what is labelled as the main headquarters building, as well as a gym and a self-help facility, all of which were among locations destroyed by recent Iranian strikes. In addition to Google Maps place markers there are dozens of reviews and user-uploaded photographs. Left: Screengrab showing “Camp Beuhring Main HQ, Bldg. 100” Google Maps label. Right: Same building seen destroyed on satellite image published by Iran’s Tasnim news agency. Bellingcat verified that this was a headquarters building by matching the flagpoles and layout in a photo published by the US military’s Defense Visual Information Distribution Service (DVIDS) showing soldiers posing in front of the building to the Google Maps satellite image. Geolocation diagram using dvids photo to verify Google Maps Buehring main headquarters location, confirming the accuracy of the Google Maps place marker. We also identified details about one of the camp’s gyms, including the building’s layout and roof structure, as well as Google reviews that indicate when it is busiest. Left: Google Maps label showing “Camp Beuhring Gym” Right: Destroyed gym building on satellite image published by Iran’s Tasnim news agency on 6 April 2026. Among the images published by CBS News in September was that of a heavily damaged tent-like structure with smoke rising from it. Bellingcat matched the location of this image to the above satellite imagery, verifying that it shows the gym building pinned on Google Maps. Exclusive images released showing damage to E-3 Sentry AWACS aircraft at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, plus damage to US military camps Arifjan and Buehring in Kuwait from Iranian strikes. Images sent to CBS by active US military personnel. (IRIB News) https://t.co/1urA44f4xz — Middle East Observer (@ME_Observer_) September 15, 2026 Left: Google Maps shows images of the gym’s interior and exterior. Right: Google Maps reviews indicate when the gym is busy (names blurred by Bellingcat). A building labeled on Google as “DPW Self-Help Center” was also destroyed at Camp Buehring. Its Google Maps listing includes opening hours, and a photo posted by a Master Sergeant in 2017 labeled “ My office in Kuwait ” shows the interior of an office. Some of the notices on the walls inside the office are legible, including what appears to be a floor plan. Left: Google maps “DPW Self-Help Center” listing. Right: Same building seen destroyed on a satellite image published by Iran’s Tasnim news agency on April 6, 2026. A Google Maps placemark labelled “ Transient Tent ” identifies a large accommodation area, while another review includes a ground-level photograph of one of the tents. The dining facility can also be seen from the inside, including information regarding meal times . Left: Google image that appears to show an accommodation area. Right: Photos of the dining facility, including information on meal times (names blurred by Bellingcat). William Goodhind of Contested Ground , a visual forensics consultancy that uses OSINT and satellite imagery to analyse military sites, said the information available on Google Maps could reveal “the camp’s layout, the division between secure and non-secure areas, confirms likely accommodation areas, and shows day/time periods of low and high activity.” Camp Arifjan A satellite image of Kuwait’s Camp Arifjan, captured by Planet on March 4, 2026 and published by the The Washington Post , shows damage to numerous structures at the base. Bellingcat compared the image with publicly available mapping data to identify two damaged facilities. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Media Trending (@tmctrending) A Google Maps listing for a lodging facility labelled “ TPE FOR ARIFJAN ” includes a soldier’s review discussing room reservations, accommodation shortages and cleaning schedules, indicating that the building was used for military housing. Although Google’s satellite imagery of the base is blurred, the facility is visible in unblurred Bing Maps imagery using coordinates obtained from its Google Maps listing. The satellite image published by The Washington Post shows heavy damage to the facility. Left and centre: Blurred Google Maps satellite image with Google review (name blurred by Bellingcat). Right: Unblurred Bing maps satellite image showing the same location. A “ 24hr Fuel Point ” tagged on Google Maps is also blurred, but when the coordinates are copied and pasted into Bing Maps a clear satellite image of the fuel station appears. This facility is also seen destroyed on the satellite imagery published by The Washington Post . Left and centre: Blurred Google Maps satellite image with Google review. Right: Unblurred Bing Maps satellite image. Bellingcat contacted Microsoft to ask why the facility was not blurred out in the Bing Maps service. A spokesperson said: “When an entity requests removal from visibility on Bing Maps, we work through our process and act accordingly.” Muwaffaq Salti Air Base Three US service members were killed in Iranian ballistic missile strikes on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on July 17, 2026. The strikes appear to have caused extensive damage to a barracks in the north of the base, with satellite imagery released by Iran showing at least 20 structures destroyed. Less than 40 metres from the nearest destroyed structure, and within the same living quarters area, Google Maps reveals the location of an “ Airman’s Attic ”. These are volunteer-run thrift shops for US Air Force personnel. A five-star review posted last year by a soldier includes a ground-level image of the facility, showing uniform drop-off points and fortifications along the perimeter. The listing provides information about the area’s use, while photographs of the shop’s exterior make it possible to match the satellite imagery to the location on the ground. A Sky News investigation also found that 80 percent of the runs shared publicly on the sporting app Strava at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base during the April ceasefire started or finished in this northern barracks. Satellite image showing damage, highlighted in red, published by Iran’s Fars News Agency. Less than 100 meters from the destroyed area, “ LSA DFAC ” is pinned on Google maps. “DFAC” is the standard US military acronym for “dining facility”, according to Stars and Stripes . Several Google reviews also discuss the steak being served in this location. Left: Google reviews for the dining facility (names blurred by Bellingcat). Right: Google Earth satellite image with the Airman’s Attic and dining facility visible in the area targeted by Iran. Al Udeid Air Base Similar mapping information is available for Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, the largest US military installation in the Middle East. The base appears unblurred on Google Maps and entries on the platform identify the functions of numerous buildings. These include lodging facilities , which videos and reviews indicate are used by US Air Force crews and show the interior layout of the facility. Google reviews for “Al Udeid Lodging” indicate the presence of US Air Force crews (names blurred by Bellingcat). Meanwhile, Russia’s Yandex Maps details the site of two cinemas, a bar and a school on the base. This appears to match information provided on Google Maps. While Al Udeid Air Base was damaged during Iranian attacks earlier this year, the areas that were struck do not appear to be among those listed on Google. Business Insider reported that a geodesic dome that housed secure communications equipment was hit in the strikes. ABC News detailed how another building had been damaged near the centre of the base. Google Maps shows a large warehouse-like structure at the location where ABC News reported this strike. A New Reality in the Middle East Former US Air Force targeting specialist Wes J. Bryant said the problem facing US bases in the Middle East reflected a broader assumption within the military that bases in allied countries were safe from serious attack. He said the belief that these were rear-area bases where “nothing’s going to happen out here” was a fundamental miscalculation, and that the Google Maps issue was an example of the military failing to account for that vulnerability. Matthew Savill, Director of Military Sciences at the Royal United Services Institute, said Western militaries do not have consistent policies governing what information can be publicly posted about sensitive sites. He said the issue needs to be considered before a conflict begins, rather than when attacks are already underway. “The start point should be, can we enforce operational security discipline?” Savill pointed to restrictions already in place at some UK military facilities, including Faslane, a naval base that houses the UK’s nuclear submarines, where he said personnel are not permitted to use mobile phones on site. Savill told Bellingcat that the different pieces of data available on Google Maps, even if outdated, provided a “pattern of life” about US bases in the Middle East. But he added that the use of Google to help with the military targeting of Western bases is not new, saying he encountered the issue while deployed to Iraq more than 20 years ago. “When I was in Iraq, we knew for a fact that insurgents and militants had been using commercial imagery, including Google Earth, to try and map our bases,” he said. “We have known for more than 20 years that there is a vulnerability that if you don’t stop the collection and layering of data early on, that your bases can be heavily mapped.” The use of open-source information to support military targeting has been documented in Ukraine. In 2022, Foreign Policy detailed how Ukrainian private intelligence company Molfar used photographs of Russian soldiers published by Russian media alongside Google Earth satellite imagery to identify their location. Molfar passed its findings to Ukrainian intelligence, and the site was subsequently struck by the Ukrainian military. The security risks of publicly mapping military installations were recognised by the US military in 2008, when the Pentagon banned Google’s Street View from documenting the interiors of its bases. Since the Iran war started, US military commanders have also warned service members about posting photographs and videos from bases after Iranian attacks, cautioning that such footage could help Iran assess the effects of its strikes. Iranian attacks have forced US personnel to evacuate many additional locations that were deemed too vulnerable to further strikes. In total, 23 US service members have been killed and 865 wounded in the US-Iran war, according to the Pentagon . Bellingcat’s Jake Godin, Charlotte Maher and Merel Zoet contributed to this report. In September, CBS News obtained new images of the aftermath of attacks on US bases in the Middle East from active service members. One told the news channel: “This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public. “We’re standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face,” they added.

While reports have detailed how Iran used Russian intelligence, including satellite imagery, to identify US troops, ships and aircraft, Bellingcat found that publicly available mapping platforms also reveal detailed and potentially sensitive information about US military bases in the Middle East. 

Google Maps and other online mapping services contain dozens of labels identifying facilities including headquarters, accommodation, gyms and fuel points. Publicly available photographs and videos, including material published by the US military, provide further details about how these facilities are used.

Experts told Bellingcat that such information could have helped inform Iranian targeting decisions by revealing where personnel gather and how bases operate. However, they cautioned that Iran would also have had access to other sources of intelligence. Reporting from Reuters earlier this year also highlighted how US officials believed commercially available location data was being used to target US troops in war zones.

The bases examined by Bellingcat are not secret and have operated for years in a region where US forces maintained a strong sense of security. Joseph Jarnecki, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, said the US had been able to maintain aerial superiority and was understood to have significant air defence capabilities, but that Iran’s missile and drone campaign has undermined both assumptions. 

Iranian strikes have damaged at least 20 US military sites across Qatar, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq and Saudi Arabia since the conflict began in February this year.

Governments can request that Google blur or remove sensitive information from its services and Google publishes data on government requests for content removal.

Bellingcat contacted the US Department of Defense who asked us to reach out to CENTCOM about the details in this story. We also contacted Google. However, we did not receive responses to questions from these respondents before publication.

We examined four of the largest and most heavily affected US military installations by Iran’s missile and drone campaign: Camp Buehring and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait, Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan and Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. At each one, we found publicly available Google Maps information providing details about facilities inside the bases and how they are used.

A map detailing four US bases that were attacked by Iran during 2026 conflict. Camp Buehring

At Camp Buehring in Kuwait, Google Maps identifies what is labelled as the main headquarters building, as well as a gym and a self-help facility, all of which were among locations destroyed by recent Iranian strikes. In addition to Google Maps place markers there are dozens of reviews and user-uploaded photographs.

Left: Screengrab showing “Camp Beuhring Main HQ, Bldg. 100” Google Maps label. Right: Same building seen destroyed on satellite image published by Iran’s Tasnim news agency.

Bellingcat verified that this was a headquarters building by matching the flagpoles and layout in a photo published by the US military’s Defense Visual Information Distribution Service (DVIDS) showing soldiers posing in front of the  building to the Google Maps satellite image.

Geolocation diagram using dvids photo to verify Google Maps Buehring main headquarters location, confirming the accuracy of the Google Maps place marker.

We also identified details about one of the camp’s gyms, including the building’s layout and roof structure, as well as Google reviews that indicate when it is busiest.

Left: Google Maps label showing “Camp Beuhring Gym” Right: Destroyed gym building on satellite image published by Iran’s Tasnim news agency on 6 April 2026.

Among the images published by CBS News in September was that of a heavily damaged tent-like structure with smoke rising from it. Bellingcat matched the location of this image to the above satellite imagery, verifying that it shows the gym building pinned on Google Maps.

Exclusive images released showing damage to E-3 Sentry AWACS aircraft at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, plus damage to US military camps Arifjan and Buehring in Kuwait from Iranian strikes. Images sent to CBS by active US military personnel. (IRIB News) https://t.co/1urA44f4xz

— Middle East Observer (@ME_Observer_) September 15, 2026
Left: Google Maps shows images of the gym’s interior and exterior. Right: Google Maps reviews indicate when the gym is busy (names blurred by Bellingcat).

A building labeled on Google as “DPW Self-Help Center” was also destroyed at Camp Buehring. Its Google Maps listing includes opening hours, and a photo posted by a Master Sergeant in 2017 labeled “My office in Kuwait” shows the interior of an office. Some of the notices on the walls inside the office are legible, including what appears to be a floor plan.

Left: Google maps “DPW Self-Help Center” listing. Right: Same building seen destroyed on a satellite image published by Iran’s Tasnim news agency on April 6, 2026.

A Google Maps placemark labelled “Transient Tent” identifies a large accommodation area, while another review includes a ground-level photograph of one of the tents. The dining facility can also be seen from the inside, including information regarding meal times.

Left: Google image that appears to show an accommodation area. Right: Photos of the dining facility, including information on meal times (names blurred by Bellingcat).

William Goodhind of Contested Ground, a visual forensics consultancy that uses OSINT and satellite imagery to analyse military sites, said the information available on Google Maps could reveal “the camp’s layout, the division between secure and non-secure areas, confirms likely accommodation areas, and shows day/time periods of low and high activity.”

Camp Arifjan

A satellite image of Kuwait’s Camp Arifjan, captured by Planet on March 4, 2026 and published by the The Washington Post, shows damage to numerous structures at the base. Bellingcat compared the image with publicly available mapping data to identify two damaged facilities.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Media Trending (@tmctrending)

A Google Maps listing for a lodging facility labelled “TPE FOR ARIFJAN” includes a soldier’s review discussing room reservations, accommodation shortages and cleaning schedules, indicating that the building was used for military housing. Although Google’s satellite imagery of the base is blurred, the facility is visible in unblurred Bing Maps imagery using coordinates obtained from its Google Maps listing. The satellite image published by The Washington Post shows heavy damage to the facility.

Left and centre: Blurred Google Maps satellite image with Google review (name blurred by Bellingcat). Right: Unblurred Bing maps satellite image showing the same location.

A “24hr Fuel Point” tagged on Google Maps is also blurred, but when the coordinates are copied and pasted into Bing Maps a clear satellite image of the fuel station appears. This facility is also seen destroyed on the satellite imagery published by The Washington Post.

Left and centre: Blurred Google Maps satellite image with Google review. Right: Unblurred Bing Maps satellite image.

Bellingcat contacted Microsoft to ask why the facility was not blurred out in the Bing Maps service. A spokesperson said: “When an entity requests removal from visibility on Bing Maps, we work through our process and act accordingly.”

Muwaffaq Salti Air Base

Three US service members were killed in Iranian ballistic missile strikes on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on July 17, 2026. The strikes appear to have caused extensive damage to a barracks in the north of the base, with satellite imagery released by Iran showing at least 20 structures destroyed.

Less than 40 metres from the nearest destroyed structure, and within the same living quarters area, Google Maps reveals the location of an “Airman’s Attic”. These are volunteer-run thrift shops for US Air Force personnel. 

A five-star review posted last year by a soldier includes a ground-level image of the facility, showing uniform drop-off points and fortifications along the perimeter. The listing provides information about the area’s use, while photographs of the shop’s exterior make it possible to match the satellite imagery to the location on the ground.

A Sky News investigation also found that 80 percent of the runs shared publicly on the sporting app Strava at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base during the April ceasefire started or finished in this northern barracks.

Satellite image showing damage, highlighted in red, published by Iran’s Fars News Agency.

Less than 100 meters from the destroyed area, “LSA DFAC” is pinned on Google maps. “DFAC” is the standard US military acronym for “dining facility”, according to Stars and Stripes. Several Google reviews also discuss the steak being served in this location.

Left: Google reviews for the dining facility (names blurred by Bellingcat). Right: Google Earth satellite image with the Airman’s Attic and dining facility visible in the area targeted by Iran. Al Udeid Air Base

Similar mapping information is available for Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, the largest US military installation in the Middle East. 

The base appears unblurred on Google Maps and entries on the platform identify the functions of numerous buildings. These include lodging facilities, which videos and reviews indicate are used by US Air Force crews and show the interior layout of the facility.

Google reviews for “Al Udeid Lodging” indicate the presence of US Air Force crews (names blurred by Bellingcat).

Meanwhile, Russia’s Yandex Maps details the site of two cinemas, a bar and a school on the base. This appears to match information provided on Google Maps.

While Al Udeid Air Base was damaged during Iranian attacks earlier this year, the areas that were struck do not appear to be among those listed on Google. 

Business Insider reported that a geodesic dome that housed secure communications equipment was hit in the strikes. ABC News detailed how another building had been damaged near the centre of the base. Google Maps shows a large warehouse-like structure at the location where ABC News reported this strike.

A New Reality in the Middle East

Former US Air Force targeting specialist Wes J. Bryant said the problem facing US bases in the Middle East reflected a broader assumption within the military that bases in allied countries were safe from serious attack. He said the belief that these were rear-area bases where “nothing’s going to happen out here” was a fundamental miscalculation, and that the Google Maps issue was an example of the military failing to account for that vulnerability.

Matthew Savill, Director of Military Sciences at the Royal United Services Institute, said Western militaries do not have consistent policies governing what information can be publicly posted about sensitive sites. He said the issue needs to be considered before a conflict begins, rather than when attacks are already underway. “The start point should be, can we enforce operational security discipline?” Savill pointed to restrictions already in place at some UK military facilities, including Faslane, a naval base that houses the UK’s nuclear submarines, where he said personnel are not permitted to use mobile phones on site.

Savill told Bellingcat that the different pieces of data available on Google Maps, even if outdated, provided a “pattern of life” about US bases in the Middle East. But he added that the use of Google to help with the military targeting of Western bases is not new, saying he encountered the issue while deployed to Iraq more than 20 years ago.

“When I was in Iraq, we knew for a fact that insurgents and militants had been using commercial imagery, including Google Earth, to try and map our bases,” he said. “We have known for more than 20 years that there is a vulnerability that if you don’t stop the collection and layering of data early on, that your bases can be heavily mapped.” 

The use of open-source information to support military targeting has been documented in Ukraine. In 2022, Foreign Policy detailed how Ukrainian private intelligence company Molfar used photographs of Russian soldiers published by Russian media alongside Google Earth satellite imagery to identify their location. Molfar passed its findings to Ukrainian intelligence, and the site was subsequently struck by the Ukrainian military.

The security risks of publicly mapping military installations were recognised by the US military in 2008, when the Pentagon banned Google’s Street View from documenting the interiors of its bases. Since the Iran war started, US military commanders have also warned service members about posting photographs and videos from bases after Iranian attacks, cautioning that such footage could help Iran assess the effects of its strikes.

Iranian attacks have forced US personnel to evacuate many additional locations that were deemed too vulnerable to further strikes. 

In total, 23 US service members have been killed and 865 wounded in the US-Iran war, according to the Pentagon.

items.title: GhostMap: The Android flaw that crashes your phone before you open the app
items.summary: Bitdefender Labs researchers found that installing a specially crafted app can leave an Android phone stuck in a crash loop, even if you never open it or grant it a single permission. The app contains no code and never needs to run.

items.title: One Hacker Uses 12 AI Agents to Breach Taiwan’s Emergency Services and Steal Sensitive Data
items.summary: A single operator in Taiwan built a team of 12 AI agents and used it to attack hundreds of organizations in 11 countries. The campaign hit emergency services, banks, universities, and military systems. It led to confirmed theft of medical data and personal records. The setup, named BOSSAI, shows how one person with rented GPUs and open-source tools can now run a campaign that once needed a full team. Some of the agents wrote code, some scanned websites, and some carried out the attacks. The operator sat in the middle and passed results between them. Analysts at Acronis Threat Research Unit identified the campaign after finding what looked like a misconfigured development server. It turned out to be a full attack platform with more than 90,000 files, about 9GB of logs, chat histories, exploit tools, and victim data. Acronis calls this kind of actor an “AI-augmented threat,” because the activity looks like a state-backed group but comes from one person, as Acronis explains in its full report. One Hacker Uses 12 AI Agents The mesh had 12 agents, but only nine were active. Builder agents such as Grok, OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex set up servers, DNS, and proxies. Attack agents such as Hermes, Cursor, Trae, and CyberStrike scanned targets and wrote exploits. Hermes did most of the work, with about 95 sessions and 18,311 messages. The agents did not talk to each other. The operator copied output from one tool and pasted it into the next. In one case, a scanner called HalberdStrike checked a Taiwanese emergency-services site. The BOSSAI mesh is composed of 12 AI agents working together in different roles (Source – Acronis) Hermes turned the findings into a report, and the operator pasted it into Cursor with the order to exploit the flaws. Cursor then carried out the attack. The agents were linked to security tools through MCP servers, including HexStrike AI, a Kali Linux server, and a Ghidra bridge. Earlier coverage of the HexStrike AI framework shows how this kind of tool lets AI models run scanners such as Nmap on their own. Attack traffic went out through proxies, and the main node ran on a server at 112[.]121[.]185[.]218. The damage in Taiwan was serious. A Taipei fire-department patient-care platform exposed ECG readings, ambulance video, and vital signs from 2018, with no login needed. Agents also pulled case records from a city 119 dispatch system, covering seven districts. Other victims included a lender with 16 SQL injection points and a fire-dispatch vendor whose database panel still used default root credentials. Outside Taiwan, the agents collected about 206,800 residential phone records in Mexico. In Thailand they found 489 targets across 45 universities and pulled data from three of them. Why the AI Agents Struggled and What It Means for Defenders The campaign was far from smooth. Commercial models such as Grok 4.5 and MiniMax M3 refused to help with attacks and asked for proof of written authorization. The operator then switched to local “abliterated” models, which have their safety rules stripped out. Those models were weaker and often made mistakes. Hallucinations caused real problems. HalberdStrike flagged a failed connection as a “critical RCE,” and more than half of its high-severity findings were false positives. Since the operator told the agents to work without asking questions, Hermes also walked away from a Honduran military system, judging it out of scope. Still, the agents worked well where basic security was weak. Old open ports, unpatched Oracle databases, and default passwords were the easy wins. The BOSSAI mesh in further detail (Source – Acronis) Where login checks and filtering held, the agents failed. Acronis notes that hiding behind obscurity no longer helps when an agent can test hundreds of sites at once. This fits a wider trend. Anthropic recently warned that AI agents can automate every stage of a cyberattack, though humans still pick targets. The first large-scale AI-driven espionage case from 2025 showed Claude doing most of an intrusion with little human input. Researchers have also seen agents try SQL injection and path traversal on their own when normal methods failed. Defenders should patch exposed databases, remove default credentials, and close old ports. They should also put login checks in front of every API, including those that serve dispatch and medical data. The same agents that find flaws quickly will keep finding them until those basics are fixed. Acronis also tied the activity to one person in Hualien City, Taiwan. The operator reused business branding, a GitHub account, and a home IP across both legitimate and attack servers. The researchers assess this with high confidence. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Indicator IP 112[.]121[.]185[.]218 IP 156[.]240[.]109[.]26 IP 49[.]158[.]237[.]136 IP 202[.]160[.]76[.]153 IP 202[.]160[.]76[.]154 IP 202[.]160[.]76[.]155 IP 202[.]160[.]76[.]156 IP 202[.]160[.]76[.]157 IP 202[.]160[.]76[.]174 Domain vps[.]xs1[.]ccwu[.]cc Domain xss[.]xs1[.]ccwu[.]cc Domain c[.]xs1[.]ccwu[.]cc Domain attacker-collector[.]com Domain boss[.]jytian[.]cc[.]cd Domain gdp[.]gasjy[.]kdns[.]fr Domain gds[.]gasjy[.]kdns[.]fr Domain 888[.]bossjy[.]kdns[.]fr Domain ssh[.]gputw[.]ai Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. items.title: Pluralistic: Without CDA 230, Facebook will own the internet forever (05 Nov 2026)
items.summary: Today's links Without CDA 230, Facebook will own the internet forever : Small, well-managed online communities are especially vulnerable to legal threats. Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : "Perfect Thing"; Recruiters tell students Iraq war is over; Toothpick Final Fantasy replicas; "Eleanor & Park"; Voter Suppression Trail; "Science Comics Computers." Upcoming appearances : Kilkenny, Courtenay, Vancouver, Folkestone, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. Without CDA 230, Facebook will own the internet forever ( permalink ) The road to hell is paved with the depraved indifference to badly considered tech policy. The internet is one of those charismatic hyperobjects that wraps around our lives in myriad ways, so tech policy changes have a big blast radius. This isn't a counsel of despair. I firmly believe that we can make tech policy, and furthermore, that we must , but that policy has to be crafted in a way that's mindful of collateral damage. Take scraping. Most creative workers are rightly furious at the palpable glee of tech bosses, who want to take everything we've made in order to train models whose express purpose is to destroy our livelihoods and transfer our wages to AI companies and the media companies they sell to. This is an entirely correct thing to be angry about. But many of my peers and comrades think the answer to this is to ban scraping, which is a terrible idea. Scraping is how we make search engines. If you want Google to be the last search engine we ever get then by all means, change the rules so you need licenses to make transient copies of the web. There's only one company with deep-enough pockets to secure permission from every web site operator: Google, the thrice-convicted monopolist that dominates the web so thoroughly that no one could afford to turn them down. Scraping is how we glue down the web's shifting sands. If you want to understand why the web says something today, it helps to know what it said yesterday. If we want to know how Zuck and Musk's algorithms are peddling disinformation and hatred, we need to be able to scrape their feeds. If we want to know how Amazon uses surveillance data to price-gouge shoppers, we need to scrape its prices. If we want to know how Uber cheats its most economically desperate drivers with lowball wage offers, we need to scrape its job listings. (It's possible to make a scraper that's so clumsy or aggressive that it crashes or destroys websites. That's a dick move. We should find people who do that and punish them; and the thing we should punish them for is trashing websites – not making transient copies of the data on those sites.) (If you want to protect creative livelihoods from AI bosses, the answer lies in labor organizing, not more copyright:) https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/21/off-the-menu/#universally-loathed The point is that while tech bosses are some of the worst, most eminently guillotineable monsters history has produced, tech is important to the lives of billions of perfectly nice people. If you let your rage at tech bosses overwhelm your care for those everyday people, you risk coming up with "punishments" that end up benefiting Big Tech and wrecking the lives of those normal users. For example: you may have heard people insist that we can solve our problems with Big Tech by "repealing Section 230." This is a reference to section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, a 26-word law that makes users responsible for their speech, while insulating the platforms that facilitate that speech from liability: https://www.techdirt.com/2020/06/23/hello-youve-been-referred-here-because-youre-wrong-about-section-230-communications-decency-act/ Here's what that means: say one user accuses another user of violating their rights through their words (libelling them, invading their privacy, etc). The wronged party can sue the person they're accusing of harming them, but they can't sue the social media platform, message board provider, hosting company, DNS provider (etc etc) for their role in hosting and transmitting the unlawful speech. At the same time, CDA 230 allows all these "intermediaries" (social media platforms, hosting companies, message board providers, etc etc) to take down or otherwise moderate content that they deem offensive, without creating an obligation to police all of their users' speech. CDA 230 grew out of lawsuits in the 1990s where online companies that took any action to remove offensive or unlawful speech were thereafter obliged to take down all unlawful speech. The lawfulness or unlawfulness of speech isn't something you can easily determine: for example, determining whether one user libeled another user requires that you find out whether the allegedly libelous speech is true . There's no way that a forum moderator can know that – it's the kind of thing you need a judge, a jury and a trial to figure out. The result of these lawsuits was that most platforms decided they wouldn't take down any speech (so as to avoid creating an obligation to police all user speech), while a minority of platforms simply removed anything that anyone might find offensive. It was a mess: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratton_Oakmont,_Inc._v._Prodigy_Services_Co. CDA 230 fixed that. CDA 230 is how an individual or a small organization can host its own Mastodon or Bluesky servers, its own message boards, etc. It's these "smallhosts" that are the primary beneficiaries of CDA 230, not the Big Tech companies that 230's opponents hope to target by reforming or repealing 230. Big Tech would be happy to see CDA 230 repealed. Mark Zuckerberg has repeatedly called for CDA 230 to be deleted, because he thinks that Meta could hire enough moderators (or use enough AI) that they could avoid being ensnared in a lot of frivolous litigation, and when legal threats did land, Zuck's army of lawyers could readily see them off: https://cepr.net/publications/repealing-section-230-giving-mark-zuckerberg-what-he-wants/ Big Tech's biggest fear isn't a repeal of CDA 230: it's mass defection of its users to smaller, independent services that are more responsive to users' needs. Zuck doesn't care if we get a new law that would make it impossible for another #MeToo to take off! This is on my mind this week because of the way that intermediary liability has nearly destroyed an online community that I helped found, way back in the early 1990s. The community is a small arts organization that I joined as a teenager. The organization sent out a quarterly newsletter, which I devoured as soon as it arrived in my mailbox. I wanted more! Without CDA 230, Facebook will own the internet forever (permalink)

The road to hell is paved with the depraved indifference to badly considered tech policy. The internet is one of those charismatic hyperobjects that wraps around our lives in myriad ways, so tech policy changes have a big blast radius.

This isn't a counsel of despair. I firmly believe that we can make tech policy, and furthermore, that we must, but that policy has to be crafted in a way that's mindful of collateral damage.

Take scraping. Most creative workers are rightly furious at the palpable glee of tech bosses, who want to take everything we've made in order to train models whose express purpose is to destroy our livelihoods and transfer our wages to AI companies and the media companies they sell to.

This is an entirely correct thing to be angry about. But many of my peers and comrades think the answer to this is to ban scraping, which is a terrible idea.

Scraping is how we make search engines. If you want Google to be the last search engine we ever get then by all means, change the rules so you need licenses to make transient copies of the web. There's only one company with deep-enough pockets to secure permission from every web site operator: Google, the thrice-convicted monopolist that dominates the web so thoroughly that no one could afford to turn them down.

Scraping is how we glue down the web's shifting sands. If you want to understand why the web says something today, it helps to know what it said yesterday. If we want to know how Zuck and Musk's algorithms are peddling disinformation and hatred, we need to be able to scrape their feeds. If we want to know how Amazon uses surveillance data to price-gouge shoppers, we need to scrape its prices. If we want to know how Uber cheats its most economically desperate drivers with lowball wage offers, we need to scrape its job listings.

(It's possible to make a scraper that's so clumsy or aggressive that it crashes or destroys websites. That's a dick move. We should find people who do that and punish them; and the thing we should punish them for is trashing websites – not making transient copies of the data on those sites.)

(If you want to protect creative livelihoods from AI bosses, the answer lies in labor organizing, not more copyright:)

https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/21/off-the-menu/#universally-loathed

The point is that while tech bosses are some of the worst, most eminently guillotineable monsters history has produced, tech is important to the lives of billions of perfectly nice people. If you let your rage at tech bosses overwhelm your care for those everyday people, you risk coming up with "punishments" that end up benefiting Big Tech and wrecking the lives of those normal users.

For example: you may have heard people insist that we can solve our problems with Big Tech by "repealing Section 230." This is a reference to section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, a 26-word law that makes users responsible for their speech, while insulating the platforms that facilitate that speech from liability:

https://www.techdirt.com/2020/06/23/hello-youve-been-referred-here-because-youre-wrong-about-section-230-communications-decency-act/

Here's what that means: say one user accuses another user of violating their rights through their words (libelling them, invading their privacy, etc). The wronged party can sue the person they're accusing of harming them, but they can't sue the social media platform, message board provider, hosting company, DNS provider (etc etc) for their role in hosting and transmitting the unlawful speech.

At the same time, CDA 230 allows all these "intermediaries" (social media platforms, hosting companies, message board providers, etc etc) to take down or otherwise moderate content that they deem offensive, without creating an obligation to police all of their users' speech.

CDA 230 grew out of lawsuits in the 1990s where online companies that took any action to remove offensive or unlawful speech were thereafter obliged to take down all unlawful speech. The lawfulness or unlawfulness of speech isn't something you can easily determine: for example, determining whether one user libeled another user requires that you find out whether the allegedly libelous speech is true. There's no way that a forum moderator can know that – it's the kind of thing you need a judge, a jury and a trial to figure out.

The result of these lawsuits was that most platforms decided they wouldn't take down any speech (so as to avoid creating an obligation to police all user speech), while a minority of platforms simply removed anything that anyone might find offensive. It was a mess:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratton_Oakmont,_Inc._v._Prodigy_Services_Co.

CDA 230 fixed that. CDA 230 is how an individual or a small organization can host its own Mastodon or Bluesky servers, its own message boards, etc. It's these "smallhosts" that are the primary beneficiaries of CDA 230, not the Big Tech companies that 230's opponents hope to target by reforming or repealing 230.

Big Tech would be happy to see CDA 230 repealed. Mark Zuckerberg has repeatedly called for CDA 230 to be deleted, because he thinks that Meta could hire enough moderators (or use enough AI) that they could avoid being ensnared in a lot of frivolous litigation, and when legal threats did land, Zuck's army of lawyers could readily see them off:

https://cepr.net/publications/repealing-section-230-giving-mark-zuckerberg-what-he-wants/

Big Tech's biggest fear isn't a repeal of CDA 230: it's mass defection of its users to smaller, independent services that are more responsive to users' needs. Zuck doesn't care if we get a new law that would make it impossible for another #MeToo to take off!

This is on my mind this week because of the way that intermediary liability has nearly destroyed an online community that I helped found, way back in the early 1990s.

items.title: Hackers Trick Mac Users Into Running Terminal Commands That Install Phexia Password-Stealing Malware
items.summary: A macOS malware family called Phexia is spreading through fake web pages that talk Mac users into pasting a command into Terminal. Once the command runs, the malware quietly settles on the Mac, steals the login password, and copies browser data, keychain files, and password-manager extension data. The trick is known as ClickFix. A page shows a fake verification or fix, and the user performs the dangerous step themselves. No software flaw is needed, so the usual protections have little to catch. Phexia is sold to several criminal groups, which is why more infections keep appearing. Analysts at WithSecure identified and detailed the malware in a report published on November 4, 2026. They say Phexia is a modular backdoor and information stealer that has been in use since at least late 2025. The firm has seen a growing number of infections since early 2026, which suggests more criminals are buying it. Hackers Trick Mac Users Into Running Terminal Commands In nearly every case WithSecure could examine, the infection started with a command typed into Terminal. The command used curl to download a shell script and sent it straight to bash. The script was usually named update.sh, though script.sh, clear-cache.sh, and Terminal.sh also appeared. It was hosted on random-looking subdomains that changed between waves. The team tied one July 6 infection to a typosquatted domain, which points to look-alike web addresses as a likely delivery route. The same trick has appeared in a fake CAPTCHA Mac campaign that also ended in password theft and cryptomining. Overview of the latest Phexia infection chain (Source – With Secure) The script then runs an AppleScript dropper. The dropper writes a LaunchAgent into the user’s Library folder and sets it to restart whenever it stops. The loader is stored as Base64 text inside that file, so no readable script sits on the disk. Builds from June to mid-September used a label of “com.” plus 16 lowercase letters. October builds switched to “com.Apple.” plus 16 letters, to look like a real Apple item. The capital “A” gives it away, because genuine Apple labels use lowercase. After setup, the backdoor checks in with its server and asks for more modules. A tool called dscl tests whether the entered login password is correct, and a fake “System Preferences” prompt can keep asking until the right one is typed. The password is saved in a hidden file named .passphrase. WithSecure saw this happen anywhere from under a minute to about eight minutes after infection. Some checks began 22 hours later and repeated on following days. With the password in hand, the stealer copies the data it wants. It reads browser “Safe Storage” keys for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi, and copies cookies, history, and saved login files. It also takes LastPass and NordPass extension stores, the login keychain, and Safari cookies. Everything is zipped and uploaded to the command server and to a second server at 62.60.226[.]50 over plain HTTP. The operators also install the XMRig Monero miner. They keep reinstalling it and changing mining pools and wallets. Similar password-grabbing tricks showed up in the MacSync macOS infostealer , so the method is clearly popular among Mac malware sellers. Polygon Blockchain Hides the Command Server The biggest recent change came in May 2026. Phexia began reading its server address from a smart contract on the Polygon blockchain, a method called EtherHiding. The loader holds no fixed server name. It asks public Polygon endpoints for the current address and then requests its next module from that host. The operator can swap in a new server by sending one blockchain transaction. Blocking a domain therefore does not remove the pointer, and the malware just looks up the next address. WithSecure saw one contract used from June 14 to October 22. A different contract appeared on October 27 and resolved to dhsbdgs[.]icu. Old infections did not move to new servers right away. Machines kept contacting an older domain for about a month after the contract changed. When a Mac was infected again, two builds ran side by side, and the earlier one kept receiving tasks for more than 20 minutes. Defenders should therefore keep old indicators in their searches and check for several LaunchAgents on one Mac. File hashes help little here, because the malware uses built-in Apple tools and every build is obfuscated differently. WithSecure recommends watching behavior instead. Look for Terminal sessions that download scripts and then launch osascript, LaunchAgents that decode Base64 into osascript, Polygon lookups from script processes, and dscl password checks. Affected users should isolate the Mac, remove every malicious LaunchAgent, reset passwords from a clean device, revoke sessions, and review password-manager and wallet exposure. The newer ClickFix abuse of Script Editor shows how fast attackers change the entry point, and the Atomic Stealer ClickFix campaign shows the same social trick. Users should never paste commands from a website into Terminal. items.title: AI-Powered Ransomware Is Coming for UK Critical Infrastructure, and Europe Is Already the Testing Ground
items.summary: Overview The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has put a date on a threat that security teams across Europe have been bracing for. In its 2026 Annual Review, The State of the Cyber Nation , the agency assesses it is highly likely that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK Critical National Infrastructure by 2028. That is not a distant, speculative scenario. It is a two-year window, and it lands alongside a second judgement. By 2028, China, Russia and other nation-states will highly likely be using AI-enabled cyber capabilities routinely to pursue geopolitical goals, with the UK facing sophisticated attacks at greater scale and speed. The review also recorded that UK and EU member states jointly attributed a December 2025 attack on Poland's energy grid to Russia's FSB Centre 16. Had it succeeded, roughly 500,000 citizens could have lost power. Europe is not watching this threat from the sidelines; it is where the playbook is being tested. Key Takeaways 2028 is the marker. The NCSC judges AI malware will highly likely be used in ransomware against UK CNI before the end of 2028. Europe's grid is already a target. Russia's FSB Centre 16 was attributed to the December 2025 attack on Poland's energy grid, and a July 2026 advisory from 18 partners in 12 countries flagged the same group exploiting vulnerable routers to reach CNI networks worldwide. China is best positioned to use AI against CNI. The NCSC rates China's activity as the most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the UK. AI speeds up old tricks rather than inventing new ones. For large organizations, 88% of incidents the NCSC handled began through just four initial access vectors. A "patch wave" is coming. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery will shrink the time defenders have between disclosure and exploitation. The gap is widening. Organizations with legacy technology and slow remediation will become the preferred targets of both states and criminals. The 2028 Warning The NCSC's assessment is precise about where AI makes the difference. It calls AI an almost certain "force multiplier" that improves reconnaissance, social engineering , vulnerability discovery and exploit development. The biggest effect, it says, will be faster and larger versions of existing tactics rather than brand-new attack vectors. Ransomware is where that acceleration hits CNI hardest. The review expects criminal adoption of AI to raise the scale and efficiency of ransomware, social engineering and exploitation. It also warns that open-source AI tools built for security researchers are likely to be repurposed to automate criminal workflows, cutting costs and raising attack volumes against less resilient targets. The agency is careful not to overstate today's reality. Its Incident Management team has begun to see attackers using AI tools, but none of the observed uses enabled a new class of attack. Human operators remain essential, and the NCSC notes that losing control of an agentic AI is likely to hinder threat actors from reaching their goals. The review's pessimistic 2028 scenario shows why that caveat may not last. In it, frontier AI is available to everyone from state actors to novice hackers, jailbroken models are sold in criminal marketplaces, and attribution becomes harder as capability spreads. It even describes a realistic possibility of an automated cyber actor operating beyond its operator's control. Cloud-controlled CNI and AI-driven robotics raise the chance that a digital compromise causes physical harm. The NCSC stresses this is an illustration of the cost of inaction, not a forecast. But it is a scenario written by the agency responsible for defending UK infrastructure, and it is set just two years out. Europe: The Proving Ground for CNI Attacks If the UK is looking at 2028, continental Europe is already living with the threat. The NCSC names Russia as the most audacious cyber threat to the UK today. GCHQ Director Anne Keast-Butler goes further in the review's foreword, warning that tactics Russia developed against Ukraine are now being turned more widely on states and their institutions. Three data points from the review frame the European picture: Poland's energy grid (December 2025). The UK and EU member states formally attributed the attack to FSB Centre 16. If successful, it could have cut electricity to around 500,000 people. Router exploitation on a global scale (July 2026). The NCSC and 18 international partners from 12 countries issued a joint advisory on FSB Centre 16 actors exploiting vulnerable routers to target CNI networks worldwide. On the same day, the UK sanctioned 24 individuals and entities tied to destructive cyber and hybrid operations, including criminals running proxy networks linked to Russian intelligence. Operational technology in crosshairs. The review points to recent attacks on programmable logic controllers (PLCs) as evidence that organizations failing to modernize are falling behind. The pattern matters for anyone running energy, water, transport or telecoms in Europe. Grids, interconnectors and supply chains cross borders, and a disruptive attack in one country can cascade into its neighbors. The review also describes how cyber threats to the UK can escalate rapidly and without warning during periods of geopolitical tension. Add AI to this mix and the timeline compresses. A state actor that today relies on patience and known router flaws could, with AI-assisted discovery and exploitation, find and weaponize new weaknesses across thousands of European edge devices far faster than defenders can patch them. China is Best Positioned to Turn AI on Critical Infrastructure While Russia is the loudest threat, the NCSC sees China as the most capable. It judges that China highly likely has both the intent and the best position to use AI against CNI and other strategic targets. Its frontier AI programmes are expected to sharpen vulnerability identification, targeting efficiency and access operations. Data sits at the center of that strategy. The review describes China collecting large volumes of information from the UK and elsewhere, then using it to train models and improve capability. In the AI era, stolen data is no longer just espionage material; it is fuel. The UK has already acted on this. In December 2025, it sanctioned two China-based firms: i-Soon, which targeted more than 80 government and private IT systems globally, and Integrity Technology Group, which the FBI has linked to the Flax Typhoon intrusions. In April 2026, the NCSC and 15 partners across nine other countries published guidance on the covert networks most China-linked actors use to hide their activity. The 2028 scenario adds a further concern: China, as a leading developer, may help spread advanced AI-cyber capability to other actors, letting them hide in the noise and making attribution harder for European defenders. AI Runs the Old Playbook, Only Faster The most useful finding in the review is also the least dramatic: attackers are still getting in through the basics. Over the past year, the NCSC received 1,831 reports of cyber attacks . Of these, 337 needed its direct support, and 80 were classed as nationally significant. For large organizations, 88% of incidents started through four initial access vectors: Exploiting public-facing applications Phishing Misuse of valid accounts Exploiting external remote services Even state-linked intrusions often used flaws for which patches already existed but had not been applied quickly enough. As the review puts it, sophisticated actors do not need to be sophisticated to gain initial access; their skill shows in what they do once inside. This is exactly where AI changes the economics. The NCSC expects AI-assisted vulnerability discovery to give attackers more chances to hit systems before owners patch them. It is urging every organization to prepare for a "patch wave": a surge of security updates across the technology stack, many of them critical, as AI exposes years of technical debt. Two further risks deserve attention: Shadow AI. Staff moving sensitive data to personal devices to use unsanctioned AI tools leaves organizations blind to where that data goes, and open to both APT groups and criminals. The widening gap. Mature, well-resourced organizations will use AI to detect and fix faster. Those running legacy systems will fall further behind and become more attractive targets. The financial stakes are already clear. UK government research cited in the review puts the annual cost of malicious cyber activity to UK organizations at about £14.7 billion. The 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover alone cost the company around £196 million in direct costs and contributed to UK GDP growing just 0.1% in Q3 2025. How the UK Is Fighting Back With AI The NCSC's answer is to meet machine-speed attacks with machine-speed defense. Several initiatives in the review stand out: Cyber Shield. A joint NCSC and DCMS programme to build a national agentic cyber defense ecosystem over five years. The NCSC supplies the platform and intelligence, while defensive agents are built by the security market and open-source community. Early phases focus on detection and blocking, where automation is already practical. Project DROMOS. Launched in 2026 by the Government Cyber Coordination Centre and the AI Security Institute, it used frontier AI models to review government codebases. Expanded into live environments, it surfaced hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities. National Detect Strategy. A pilot aiming, by 2030, to ensure defenders across critical systems can detect and respond to known vulnerabilities and attacker techniques at organizational, community and national scale. Regulation and benchmarks. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill brings new sectors into scope and adds national security powers. The new CAF Core Profile sets a minimum resilience baseline for essential services. There are early results. Under the Government Cyber Action Plan, the median time to fix domain-related vulnerabilities fell from 50 days to 8. The Early Warning service now covers 19,922 organizations, up 52% on last year. For Europe, the lesson is that partnership is now part of the defense. The review highlights the world's first AI security standard developed through ETSI, the European standards body, as proof that allies can shape AI security while the technology is still evolving. National defense at machine speed also depends on seeing adversaries before they reach the network. Groups like FSB Centre 16 and China-linked operators plan, recruit, and trade access in places most defenders never look. As AI makes attribution harder, government agencies, national CERTs, and defense bodies need intelligence that tracks threat actors across the open, deep, and dark web and connects that activity to the infrastructure being targeted. Cyble Hawk is built for exactly this. It gives national security teams sovereign threat intelligence, adversary profiling, and investigative support. That means early warning of campaigns against critical infrastructure and stronger attribution when an attack does land. Book a demo to see how your agency can move from reacting to incidents to anticipating them. Recommendations for CNI Operators in the UK and Europe The NCSC's core message is that AI did not create these weaknesses; it is exposing them faster. Operators of critical infrastructure should act on the following now: Harden the edge first. Inventory and patch internet-facing applications, VPNs, routers, and remote access services. These are the routes FSB Centre 16 and others are actively exploiting. Prepare for the patch wave. Build processes to test and deploy security updates more often, faster and across suppliers. Track time-to-remediate as a board-level metric. Kill password-based access where you can. Move privileged and remote users to phishing-resistant authentication such as passkeys, and audit valid accounts for misuse. Segment IT from OT. Limit the paths from corporate networks to PLCs and industrial control systems, and monitor those boundaries continuously. Govern AI use internally. Map what data AI tools and agents can access, what actions they can take, and how they are monitored. Close off shadow AI with approved alternatives. Rehearse recovery, not just prevention. Test ransomware response playbooks against scenarios where operational systems must run during disruption. Use the NCSC's guidance on recovering from highly disruptive attacks. Lock down the supply chain. Require baseline controls such as Cyber Essentials, or equivalent standards in EU frameworks, from suppliers with access to critical systems. Use threat intelligence that moves at AI speed. Monitor for exploitation of newly disclosed flaws, stolen credentials, and chatter about your sector, so you can act before an incident escalates. Start post-quantum planning. The NCSC wants discovery and migration planning finished by 2028, priority migrations by 2031 and full migration by 2035. Conclusion The NCSC has given Europe a deadline. By 2028, AI-powered ransomware against UK critical infrastructure moves from possibility to expectation, and state actors will be using AI as a routine part of their operations. The Poland grid attack and the global router campaign show the targeting is already in place; AI simply adds speed and scale. The agency's own framing is a "moment of choice." Organizations that modernize, patch fast, and build resilience now will be able to absorb what comes next. Those that defer will find AI exposing their technical debt faster than they can repay it. For CNI operators across the UK and Europe, the next two years are the window to close the gap. Continuous visibility into emerging vulnerabilities, active exploitation and threat actor activity will be central to staying ahead of attacks that move at machine speed. Source NCSC Annual Review 2026: The State of the Cyber Nation

On the same day, the UK sanctioned 24 individuals and entities tied to destructive cyber and hybrid operations, including criminals running proxy networks linked to Russian intelligence. 

  • Operational technology in crosshairs. The review points to recent attacks on programmable logic controllers (PLCs) as evidence that organizations failing to modernize are falling behind. 

The pattern matters for anyone running energy, water, transport or telecoms in Europe. Grids, interconnectors and supply chains cross borders, and a disruptive attack in one country can cascade into its neighbors. The review also describes how cyber threats to the UK can escalate rapidly and without warning during periods of geopolitical tension. 

Add AI to this mix and the timeline compresses. A state actor that today relies on patience and known router flaws could, with AI-assisted discovery and exploitation, find and weaponize new weaknesses across thousands of European edge devices far faster than defenders can patch them. 

China is Best Positioned to Turn AI on Critical Infrastructure 

While Russia is the loudest threat, the NCSC sees China as the most capable. It judges that China highly likely has both the intent and the best position to use AI against CNI and other strategic targets. Its frontier AI programmes are expected to sharpen vulnerability identification, targeting efficiency and access operations. 

Data sits at the center of that strategy. The review describes China collecting large volumes of information from the UK and elsewhere, then using it to train models and improve capability. In the AI era, stolen data is no longer just espionage material; it is fuel. 

The UK has already acted on this. In December 2025, it sanctioned two China-based firms: i-Soon, which targeted more than 80 government and private IT systems globally, and Integrity Technology Group, which the FBI has linked to the Flax Typhoon intrusions. In April 2026, the NCSC and 15 partners across nine other countries published guidance on the covert networks most China-linked actors use to hide their activity. 

The 2028 scenario adds a further concern: China, as a leading developer, may help spread advanced AI-cyber capability to other actors, letting them hide in the noise and making attribution harder for European defenders. 

AI Runs the Old Playbook, Only Faster 

The most useful finding in the review is also the least dramatic: attackers are still getting in through the basics. Over the past year, the NCSC received 1,831 reports of cyber attacks. Of these, 337 needed its direct support, and 80 were classed as nationally significant. 

For large organizations, 88% of incidents started through four initial access vectors: 

  1. Exploiting public-facing applications 

  1. Phishing 

  1. Misuse of valid accounts 

  1. Exploiting external remote services 

Even state-linked intrusions often used flaws for which patches already existed but had not been applied quickly enough. As the review puts it, sophisticated actors do not need to be sophisticated to gain initial access; their skill shows in what they do once inside. 

This is exactly where AI changes the economics. The NCSC expects AI-assisted vulnerability discovery to give attackers more chances to hit systems before owners patch them. It is urging every organization to prepare for a "patch wave": a surge of security updates across the technology stack, many of them critical, as AI exposes years of technical debt. 

Two further risks deserve attention: 

  • Shadow AI. Staff moving sensitive data to personal devices to use unsanctioned AI tools leaves organizations blind to where that data goes, and open to both APT groups and criminals. 

  • The widening gap. Mature, well-resourced organizations will use AI to detect and fix faster. Those running legacy systems will fall further behind and become more attractive targets. 

The financial stakes are already clear. UK government research cited in the review puts the annual cost of malicious cyber activity to UK organizations at about £14.7 billion. The 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover alone cost the company around £196 million in direct costs and contributed to UK GDP growing just 0.1% in Q3 2025. 

How the UK Is Fighting Back With AI 

The NCSC's answer is to meet machine-speed attacks with machine-speed defense. Several initiatives in the review stand out: 

  • Cyber Shield. A joint NCSC and DCMS programme to build a national agentic cyber defense ecosystem over five years. The NCSC supplies the platform and intelligence, while defensive agents are built by the security market and open-source community. Early phases focus on detection and blocking, where automation is already practical. 

  • Project DROMOS. Launched in 2026 by the Government Cyber Coordination Centre and the AI Security Institute, it used frontier AI models to review government codebases. Expanded into live environments, it surfaced hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities. 

  • National Detect Strategy. A pilot aiming, by 2030, to ensure defenders across critical systems can detect and respond to known vulnerabilities and attacker techniques at organizational, community and national scale. 

  • Regulation and benchmarks. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill brings new sectors into scope and adds national security powers. The new CAF Core Profile sets a minimum resilience baseline for essential services. 

There are early results. Under the Government Cyber Action Plan, the median time to fix domain-related vulnerabilities fell from 50 days to 8. The Early Warning service now covers 19,922 organizations, up 52% on last year. 

For Europe, the lesson is that partnership is now part of the defense. The review highlights the world's first AI security standard developed through ETSI, the European standards body, as proof that allies can shape AI security while the technology is still evolving. 

National defense at machine speed also depends on seeing adversaries before they reach the network. Groups like FSB Centre 16 and China-linked operators plan, recruit, and trade access in places most defenders never look. As AI makes attribution harder, government agencies, national CERTs, and defense bodies need intelligence that tracks threat actors across the open, deep, and dark web and connects that activity to the infrastructure being targeted. Cyble Hawk is built for exactly this. It gives national security teams sovereign threat intelligence, adversary profiling, and investigative support. That means early warning of campaigns against critical infrastructure and stronger attribution when an attack does land. Book a demo to see how your agency can move from reacting to incidents to anticipating them. 

Recommendations for CNI Operators in the UK and Europe 

The NCSC's core message is that AI did not create these weaknesses; it is exposing them faster. Operators of critical infrastructure should act on the following now: 

  1. Harden the edge first. Inventory and patch internet-facing applications, VPNs, routers, and remote access services. These are the routes FSB Centre 16 and others are actively exploiting. 

  1. Prepare for the patch wave. Build processes to test and deploy security updates more often, faster and across suppliers. Track time-to-remediate as a board-level metric. 

  1. Kill password-based access where you can. Move privileged and remote users to phishing-resistant authentication such as passkeys, and audit valid accounts for misuse. 

  1. Segment IT from OT. Limit the paths from corporate networks to PLCs and industrial control systems, and monitor those boundaries continuously. 

  1. Govern AI use internally. Map what data AI tools and agents can access, what actions they can take, and how they are monitored. Close off shadow AI with approved alternatives. 

  1. Rehearse recovery, not just prevention. Test ransomware response playbooks against scenarios where operational systems must run during disruption. Use the NCSC's guidance on recovering from highly disruptive attacks. 

  1. Lock down the supply chain. Require baseline controls such as Cyber Essentials, or equivalent standards in EU frameworks, from suppliers with access to critical systems. 

  1. Use threat intelligence that moves at AI speed. Monitor for exploitation of newly disclosed flaws, stolen credentials, and chatter about your sector, so you can act before an incident escalates. 

  1. Start post-quantum planning. The NCSC wants discovery and migration planning finished by 2028, priority migrations by 2031 and full migration by 2035. 

Conclusion 

The NCSC has given Europe a deadline. By 2028, AI-powered ransomware against UK critical infrastructure moves from possibility to expectation, and state actors will be using AI as a routine part of their operations. The Poland grid attack and the global router campaign show the targeting is already in place; AI simply adds speed and scale. 

The agency's own framing is a "moment of choice." Organizations that modernize, patch fast, and build resilience now will be able to absorb what comes next. Those that defer will find AI exposing their technical debt faster than they can repay it. 

For CNI operators across the UK and Europe, the next two years are the window to close the gap. Continuous visibility into emerging vulnerabilities, active exploitation and threat actor activity will be central to staying ahead of attacks that move at machine speed.

items.title: Hackers Use Fake Government Websites and CAPTCHA Checks to Deliver SimpleHelp Remote Access Software
items.summary: Hackers are impersonating the Israel Tax Authority through phishing emails, fake government websites, and CAPTCHA-style checks to trick employees into running SimpleHelp remote access software. The campaign targets Israeli organizations and turns an ordinary tax-document request into a possible entry point for unauthorized access. Observed since September 2026, the activity targets a business task familiar to finance, accounting, and administrative staff. Instead of receiving a tax document, recipients download an archive containing an executable. The attack reflects broader phishing campaigns abusing RMM tools, where legitimate software becomes a route into company systems. Researchers from Cato Networks identified the campaign’s delivery infrastructure and examined its use of SimpleHelp. In their November 3 research report, Cato CTRL researchers said they suspect a connection to MuddyWater, although the evidence does not establish definitive attribution. CyberIL had previously reported the activity. Hackers Use Fake Government Websites and CAPTCHA Checks The attack starts with an email claiming to come from the Israel Tax Authority. Recipients who try to enter the supposed personal account area reach a lookalike website. Its government-themed name creates a misleading connection to Israel’s official government web namespace. The page then presents a checkbox, a Continue button, and an archive password. These details make the download resemble a protected document service. Unlike fake CAPTCHA command attacks that instruct victims to paste commands into Terminal, this chain uses verification to lead users toward a ZIP download and subsequent executable launch. Attack Flow (Source – Cato Networks) Inside the archive, the supposed tax document is actually a program. One sample carries a Hebrew filename meaning “Israel Tax Authority,” extending the impersonation beyond the browser. Opening it can deploy SimpleHelp configured to connect to infrastructure controlled by the attackers. SimpleHelp is legitimate remote support software, not inherently malware. Its normal features include desktop control, terminal access, file transfers, and system diagnostics. When deployed without authorization, those same functions could let an operator inspect business systems, run commands, retrieve files, or deliver additional tools. The distinction between capability and observation matters. Cato described these functions as potential attacker uses, not confirmed actions in this campaign. Its telemetry showed a blocked request to campaign infrastructure, rather than proof that an attacker completed a remote-access session or stole information. Suspected MuddyWater Links and the Limits of the Evidence Cato’s attribution assessment rests on Israeli targeting, locally tailored impersonation, and phishing that delivers legitimate remote-access software. Earlier MuddyWater remote access operations also involved SimpleHelp, providing relevant context. However, similarities in tools and targeting support suspicion rather than conclusive identification of the operator. The infrastructure investigation also used FOFA searches for two HTTP ETag values. Researchers found eight service records associated with one IP address, including two campaign domains displaying nginx “Coming Soon” pages. Verification interface used in the tax authority lure (Source – Cato Networks) Those eight records should not be mistaken for eight separate servers or confirmed victims. Cato notified SimpleHelp on October 20, 2026, and shared server information the following day. SimpleHelp identified both samples as Remote Access Client version 5.4.5 and assessed the findings as apparent malicious use of an older release. Neither party identified evidence of a software vulnerability being exploited. That separates this campaign from earlier SimpleHelp vulnerability exploitation incidents involving compromised remote-management deployments. Here, the documented entry point was social engineering intended to persuade users to install an attacker-configured client. Cato also found no evidence that SimpleHelp’s own infrastructure had been compromised in connection with this activity.
